newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FORECAST - French polls, EMU row hurt Iberia bonds.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - French polls, EMU row hurt Iberia bonds.

text.p: The outcome of French elections on Sunday and the Bundesbank's criticism of a German government plan to revalue its official reserves will weigh most heavily on longer Iberian bonds next week, widening yield spreads against Bunds, analysts said.
Both issues fuelled speculation about a possible delay in the launch of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), which would hurt 10-year Spanish and Portuguese government bonds, they said.
Some said they expected investors to reduce their exposure to 10-year bonds and take refuge in three- or four-year bonds, less prone to the impact of the volatility of foreign markets.

"I am negative," said Giovanni Polastri, analyst with 4Cast in London. "If there are doubts about the creation of monetary union in 1999, and I think that there ought to be, then Iberian spreads (10-year Iberian bonds against Bunds) should widen."

"Considering the French elections and the row between the German government and the Bundesbank over gold reserves, both factors are negative for Bonos, especially 10-year bonds," said Henrik Lumholdt, an analyst with Bank of America in Madrid.

Spreads of 10-year Spanish government bonds, or Bonos, and Portuguese bonds, or OTs, against Bunds now stand at 76 and 63 basis points respectively, compared with historic lows of 64 and 50 basis points (bps) last week.

Analysts recalled that optimism over Portugal's prospects to join the European single currency, or euro, from the start in 1999 had been the motor for the recent drop in spreads, which have fallen from 330 and 320 bps respectively in March 1996.
Most opinion polls say the left will win second round legislative elections in France.

Germany's powerful Bundesbank and the Bonn government entered open conflict on Wednesday as the central bank rejected Bonn's plans to revalue its assets and the government said it would go ahead regardless.
"The French Socialists favour the euro, like the centre-right, but they do not favour a policy of fiscal austerity. This increases the risk of a delay in the euro," said Lumholdt.
Valentin Fernandez of Credit Lyonnais in Madrid said: "The Socialists may need the help of the Communists, who are not very friendly towards the euro."

Polastri said: "The worst scenario would be a victory of the left. If the centre-right wins, there could be some support at the shorter end, but the standoff between the Bundesbank and Bonn is likely to continue and this is bad for Iberian bonds."

He added: "If the left wins, the spread of 10-year Bonos against Bunds should exceed 80 basis points, perhaps 85. If the centre-right wins, spreads could initially stand at around 70 bps and then widen to around 80 bps amid nervousness over EMU."

Nuno Godinho of Deutsche Morgan Grenfell said: "The wide spread between Portuguese bonds and Bonos is due largely to the lack of liquidity in February 2007 Portuguese bonds, and the spread could widen further."
A fixed income analyst said he expected the spread between 10-year bonds and Bonos to stand at around 10 bps next week.

Fernandez said he recommended that investors should reduce their holdings of 10-year bonds and focus increasingly on three- and four-year bonds, which would be more likely to resist a delay in the launch of the euro.
He said there could be a slight steepening of the Spanish and Portuguese yield curves next week.
Lumholdt said that selling pressure on the peseta next week would weigh on shorter Bonos prices.
"I think the peseta will not fall below 85 (per mark), but if it breaks through that barrier it would be bad for shorter bonds," Valentin Fernandez said.
Godinho said: "I am not expecting a big drop in the escudo (against the mark)."
